title: Speaking Part 1 — react, answer, expand
note:
The ladder is the school's formula: react, answer, then expand with a reason, an example and a contrast. It is not new to this repo — part1-structure.json's phraseBank already holds it as five steps, and this file is that bank turned into something a student does rather than reads.

THE REACTION IS PREPENDED. Level 1 is the bare answer a student gives unprompted; round 1 puts a reaction in FRONT of it. The screen performs the rule, which is the one thing a phrase list cannot do. Every other move is appended.

Every level is written in full by a person. The engine never composes an answer — it only chooses which level to show. Three voices run the same ladder at the same depth, so switching changes whose life it is, not how developed the answer is.

icon and color are deliberately absent. The old bank stored an emoji and a hex per step, and presentation inside a data file is how a page ends up carrying five saturated hues from no palette in this product.

x.name: React
x.hint: how you feel about the question, before you answer it

e.name: Example
e.hint: one specific thing from your own life

c.name: Contrast
c.hint: the other side, so the answer sounds balanced

phraseBank.heading: Reacting — not keen
phrases: I can't say I'm keen on…
I've never been that bothered about…
I'd rather not, if I'm honest…

phraseBank.heading: Reacting — fronted, and worth two criteria
phraseBank.note: These are clefts. They mark the discourse and count as complex structures at the same time.
phrases: The thing I love about… is…
If there's one thing I…, it's…

tip: Don't memorise answers. Start with your reaction, develop the idea, add an example, show some balance. An answer that follows the shape sounds natural; an answer that recites it does not.

rounds.prompt: Nine words, and you've already finished. Any of these reactions works — pick the one that sounds like you.

options.t: Oh, Saturdays are easily the best part of my week.
options.note: Interjection plus a superlative. The quickest reaction there is, and it buys you two seconds to think.

options.t: To be honest, I live for the weekend a bit.
options.note: A hedge. It sounds thoughtful rather than rehearsed, which is exactly what stops a formula sounding like one.

options.t: What I love about weekends is that nothing is timetabled.
options.note: A pseudo-cleft. It marks the discourse AND counts as a complex structure, so one phrase earns on two criteria.

options.t: The weekend is Saturday and Sunday.
options.why: A definition, not a reaction. The examiner knows what a weekend is; they don't know what you make of yours.

rounds.prompt: You've reacted and answered. Now expand — start with a reason.

options.t: This is mainly because we hardly see each other during the week.
I really like spending time with my friends.
options.why: This repeats the reaction and the answer at once. A reason gives the examiner something neither of them has said.

options.t: My favourite subject at school is history.
options.why: True, but it develops a question nobody asked. In Part 1 you expand the question you were given.

rounds.prompt: Keep expanding. What makes this answer yours and nobody else's?

options.t: Last Saturday, for instance, we walked along the seafront for about three hours and didn't plan any of it.
We do lots of different things together.
options.why: Still general. An example names something — when, where, how long. That is what stops an answer sounding like anyone's.

options.t: Friendship is very important in people's lives.
options.why: A statement about the world, not about you. Part 1 is the one part of the exam that asks about your own life.

rounds.prompt: One last move, and it's the one that makes an answer sound balanced.

options.t: That said, if there's a test coming up I end up stuck at my desk instead.
And that's basically what I do at the weekend.
options.why: Signing off is not a move. The examiner is waiting for the other side, not for you to stop.

options.t: On Sundays I usually do my homework as well.
options.why: Another example, not a contrast. A contrast admits something that cuts against what you've just said.
